ABSTRACT

Deep learning-based fault diagnosis has achieved significant success in intelligent industrial monitoring. However, diagnosing faults in fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (FW-UAVs) under limited data conditions remains challenging because of scarce fault data, complex spatiotemporal dynamics of flight signals, and difficulty in simultaneously capturing global dependencies and local topology evolution patterns. To address these challenges, we propose a novel dynamic graph-enhanced multi-scale attention network (DGMANet) for robust fault diagnosis of FW-UAVs under small-sample conditions. Specifically, DGMANet integrates a dynamic graph enhancement mechanism that models localized topological dependencies and adaptive inter-feature correlations, thereby enabling effective structural feature learning even with limited data. A multi-scale attention module is incorporated to extract hierarchical global dependencies, which permits the model to concentrate on salient temporal patterns across multiple resolutions. Furthermore, an adaptive feature aggregation strategy is introduced to fuse local and global representations, enhancing feature complementarity while suppressing noise and redundancy. Extensive experiments on four real-world flight datasets demonstrate that DGMANet consistently outperforms existing baselines in small-sample scenarios, validating its effectiveness and generalization capability in resource-constrained UAV monitoring scenarios.
1. Introduction

In recent years, driven by rapid advances in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology, UAVs have been widely adopted in environmental monitoring $[1]$ , intelligent transportation $[2]$ , agriculture $[3]$ , and intelligent control technology $[4]$ owing to their structural flexibility and cost-effectiveness. UAVs currently represent a primary research focus. Nonetheless, uncertainties during mission execution considerably increase the risk of UAV malfunctions $[5]$ . These uncertainties impose stringent demands on reliability and stability, especially in safety-critical applications requiring advanced control systems and robust fault detection. Compared to other UAV types, FW-UAVs possess more complex configurations and typically serve specialized, demanding tasks. Their intricate subsystems may adversely affect critical performance metrics [6] and can lead to severe property damage and safety hazards when faults occur. Therefore, flight-data-based fault diagnosis for FW-UAVs holds considerable practical significance.
Fault diagnosis technology is essential for improving system stability and reducing failure rates in UAVs. A comprehensive review of existing methods categorizes them into four groups:

1. Hardware redundancy-based methods. These approaches improve UAV reliability by integrating redundant components, thereby substantially enhancing system robustness [7]. However, redundancy increases costs, system complexity, and hardware-fault risk. Moreover, added weight and volume reduce payload capacity, limiting practical applications.

2. Expert knowledge-based methods. These methods provide enhanced interpretability and lower false alarm rates relative to hardware-based techniques. Some implementations apply hidden Markov models (HMMs) [8] and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems (ANFIS) [9] to diagnose navigation sensor faults. However, reliance on subjective and limited expert knowledge restricts scalability and generalization.

3. Model-driven methods. Valued for computational efficiency and reliability, these techniques depend on precise mathematical models. For example, a differential flatness-based approach detects sensor and actuator faults by comparing analytical and actual measurements to compute residuals $[10]$ . Another framework uses an improved Kalman filter to update neural network parameters in real time $[11]$ . Despite these advantages, modeling inaccuracies often result in increased false positives.

4. Data-driven methods. These approaches have become prominent for learning from historical flight data without explicit models. Their adaptability and minimal expert-knowledge requirement render them suitable for complex nonlinear systems. One method extracts spatiotemporal features via neural networks and employs Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for anomaly recovery $[12]$ . Another integrates discrete wavelet transforms with deep neural networks for time–frequency fault diagnosis $[13]$ . Although data-driven approaches dominate UAV fault diagnosis research, they rely heavily on large-scale fault data, which are rarely available in real-world UAV operations.

In real-world UAV operations, UAV fault data are difficult to obtain owing to the uniqueness of missions and the operational risks and safety constraints involved. To address this challenge, existing approaches frequently generate synthetic fault datasets via simulation and utilize techniques such as time–frequency feature extraction and domain adaptation to improve detection performance $[14,15]$ . Additionally, some studies acquire real fault data by injecting faults during flight tests or simulating specific fault conditions to obtain representative training data $[16,17]$ . However, simulated data do not capture actual dynamic behaviors and noise characteristics. Conversely, real-time fault injection incurs substantial costs and operational risks, especially in complex environments where UAVs maintain stable control under varying conditions. Consequently, data-driven UAV fault diagnosis faces a critical small-sample learning challenge. To address this issue, various deep-learning methods have been explored. The Siamese Hybrid Neural Network (SHNN) combines one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D-CNN) for spatial feature extraction with LSTM networks for temporal modeling, utilizing distance-based similarity measures for classification $[18]$ . To further enhance small-sample performance, multi-scale CNN architectures integrating adaptive learning mechanisms, such as Kalman filter-enhanced optimization $[19]$ , and time-frequency feature-based encoder-decoder networks $[20]$ have been proposed. Moreover, recent studies have incorporated attention mechanisms to enhance discriminative feature learning. The adaptive Siamese Network (ASN) employs channel-wise attention modules that dynamically recalibrate multi-channel feature responses to reinforce spatial-temporal coupling $[21]$ . Similarly, the heterogeneous deep multitask learning (HDMTL) framework combines CNN and LSTM modules with adaptive attention-based feature fusion $[22]$ .

Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a robust paradigm for modeling complex relational structures in multivariate systems; in UAV-related applications, graph-based architectures have proven effective at capturing inter-component dependencies through adaptive topology learning. Several GNN-based approaches have been developed specifically for UAV fault diagnosis. DIGPGNN [23] constructs a feature-similarity-based directed graph and employs adaptive bidirectional aggregation to enhance homophilic neighborhood representations, moreover introducing an efficient graph transformer with global self-attention to connect distant homophilic nodes. CLGNN $[24]$ models sensor-relation graphs with causal interventions during feature extraction to suppress non-causal components and improve interpretability. He et al. $[25]$ constructed cross-component sensor-relation graphs and combined spatial graph attention with GRU networks to capture temporal dynamics. Li et al. $[26]$ introduced MFFTD, which leverages multi-scale convolution and LSTM on temporal dynamic graphs to capture spatio-temporal correlations and employs mutual information-based multi-head feature fusion to address heterogeneity imbalance. Despite these advances, most methods depend on predefined static graph structures or separate temporal modules, failing to jointly learn adaptive dynamic graphs and multi-resolution temporal patterns within a unified framework. This limitation becomes critical in small-sample scenarios wherein structural adaptability and hierarchical temporal modeling are essential for robust fault detection.

UAV flight data exhibit complex spatiotemporal dependencies and dynamic multivariate structures that challenge effective modeling. Although these methods demonstrate notable progress, they often treat spatial structural learning separately from temporal feature extraction or rely on fixed topological assumptions that may not generalize across varying operational conditions. Specifically, static graph structures fail to adapt when UAV sensor relationships evolve with flight conditions, limiting their generalization capability. Meanwhile, single-scale attention mechanisms focus on uniform temporal granularity, missing either fine-grained transient faults or long-term dynamic drifts. Furthermore, simple feature fusion strategies ignore the structural heterogeneity between graph-based spatial and sequence-based temporal features, introducing noise and redundancy. Consequently, their ability to capture the coupled evolution of spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics remains limited, especially in data-scarce environments. These observations underscore the necessity for data-efficient models with adaptive spatiotemporal representations.

To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel framework—Dynamic Graph-enhanced Multi-scale Attention Network (DGMANet)—for robust fault diagnosis in FW-UAVs under small-sample conditions. DGMANet integrates three modules to capture local and global dynamics. First, a dynamic graph construction module adaptively models localized structural dependencies and inter-feature relationships. Second, a multi-scale attention mechanism (MSAM) extracts hierarchical temporal features at multiple resolutions, enabling the network to concentrate on salient time-dependent patterns. Third, an adaptive feature aggregation module (AFAM) fuses local and global representations, enhancing complementarity while suppressing noise and redundancy. Together, these components form a cohesive architecture capable of accurately identifying faults in complex, data-scarce operational environments. The primary contributions of this work are as follows:

\- We introduce a dynamic graph construction mechanism that models localized topological dependencies and adaptive inter-feature correlations, thereby enabling structural representation learning without reliance on large-scale data.

\- We design a multi-scale attention module that extracts hierarchical temporal features and selectively emphasizes salient patterns across varying time resolutions, thus improving the capacity of the model for capturing complex temporal dynamics.

\- We implement an adaptive feature aggregation strategy to merge local and global representations, improving feature complementarity while effectively mitigating redundancy and noise in spatiotemporal signals.
\- Extensive validation on four real-world FW-UAV flight datasets demonstrates that DGMANet achieves high diagnostic accuracy.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 presents the problem formulation and details the implementation of the proposed DGMANet; Section 4 describes the experimental setup, baseline methods, analysis, ablation studies, and visualization results; and Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines potential directions for future research.

2. Related works

In this section, we provide an overview of the theoretical foundations and recent advances in small-sample UAV fault diagnosis, dynamic graph neural networks, and local and global spatiotemporal modeling.
2.1. Small-sample UAV fault diagnosis

The rapid proliferation of UAVs in complex mission environments has rendered fault diagnosis essential for ensuring system safety, autonomy, and robustness. To address limited-sample scenarios, researchers proposed an adaptive Siamese network with channel attention that identifies fault patterns from multi-channel sensor data with few-shot adaptability $[21]$ . For real-time onboard recognition, a lightweight CNN–LSTM architecture was developed and optimized for embedded platforms, enabling efficient fault cause detection directly from raw sensor signals $[27]$ . A meta-learning framework with adaptive learning rates was introduced to enhance generalization and enable rapid adaptation to new fault types with few labeled samples $[28]$ . To improve anomaly detection under heterogeneous data conditions, a hybrid multi-modal neural network was introduced that leverages attention mechanisms and soft-voting strategies for robust cross-domain fault identification $[29]$ . Furthermore, a knowledge-complementary framework was proposed to jointly exploit temporal and spatial features in identifying fault locations and severity, thereby enhancing diagnostic accuracy and generalization $[22]$ . Few-shot fault diagnosis substantially improves UAV safety and robustness in data-scarce, complex operational scenarios. Nevertheless, most existing methods rely on episodic training and support-query matching paradigms, which limit their applicability when representative samples are scarce under diverse flight conditions.
2.2. Dynamic graph neural networks

GNNs have exhibited strong capabilities in processing non-Euclidean data and modeling spatial dependencies. Early contributions introduced Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), which update node features by aggregating information from adjacent and self-nodes $[30]$ . GCNs are broadly categorized into spectral $[31]$ and spatial approaches. Spectral methods perform convolution in the graph spectral domain, whereas spatial methods extract structural features through convolution over local neighborhoods. Recent studies have leveraged GCNs for various fault diagnosis applications. Some integrate GCNs with structure analysis (SA) to convert pre-diagnostic results into association graphs for fault identification $[32]$ . Others incorporate temporal modeling via time recursive GNNs that embed recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for dynamic system monitoring $[33]$ . Multi-scale architectures, such as MS-GCN $[34]$ and MST-BGCT $[35]$ , refine the extraction of subtle spatiotemporal features by combining GCNs with iterative modules or Transformer-based encoders. Despite these advancements, the application of GCNs to small-sample fault diagnosis in FW-UAVs remains largely unexplored. Given their robust spatial modeling capabilities, GCNs hold substantial potential for capturing local topological structures and spatial pairwise dependencies in time series data, offering avenues to advance fault diagnosis performance in this challenging domain. Therefore, further research is needed to explore how temporal dynamic graphs can be applied from a global perspective to address small-sample flight fault diagnosis.
2.3. Local and global spatiotemporal modeling

Recent studies have indicated that integrating local features with global correlations substantially enhances temporal feature extraction in time series modeling [36]. FW-UAV flight data comprise multiple time-varying variables and exemplify multivariate time series data. To capture spatiotemporal dynamics from raw sensor inputs, models commonly employ combinations of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and bidirectional or unidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM/LSTM) networks, in which CNNs extract spatial features and LSTM variants capture local temporal dependencies [18,37]. Alternative to sequence-based models, some approaches transform one-dimensional time series into two-dimensional tensors to enable CNNs to capture both local and global temporal patterns simultaneously [38]. The multi-head attention architecture offers advantages in modeling long-range dependencies within time series data, making it well suited to address the complex temporal dynamics inherent in FW-UAV flight data [39]. Recent methods such as the multiscale periodic time series network (MPTSNet) integrate convolution and attention modules within a multi-scale framework to jointly model local patterns and global correlations [40]. However, LSTM-based models remain limited in capturing global temporal structures, and either strictly serial or parallel processing of local and global features can restrict their interaction, potentially resulting in the loss of critical contextual information. These limitations underscore the need for more adaptive, integrated architectures that fully exploit the spatiotemporal characteristics of FW-UAV flight data. However, single-scale attention mechanisms and simple fusion strategies fail to capture multi-granularity temporal patterns while overlooking the structural heterogeneity between spatial and temporal features. In this study, we propose a MSAM module for hierarchical temporal modeling and an AFAM module for heterogeneous spatiotemporal fusion.
3. Methodology

In this section, we first provide a systematic definition of the symbols used in the FW-UAV fault diagnosis problem. Subsequently, we present a comprehensive description of the DGMANet architecture, including the data embedding module, the dynamic graph-enhanced module (DGM), the global dependencies extractor (GDE), the MSAM module, and the AFAM module. Subsequently, the pooling and fully connected layers used for classification are detailed. A rigorous time-complexity analysis of DGMANet is also provided.
3.1. Model architecture overview

The overall DGMANet framework is illustrated in Fig. 1. Initially, DGMANet preprocesses the input time series data. Subsequently, a dual-branch architecture is adopted for feature modeling: one branch employs DGM to extract spatial-local topological structures and dynamic correlations among feature variables, while the other branch leverages GDE to capture long-range global dependencies and prominent temporal patterns. The GDE branch output is further processed by MSAM, which characterizes multi-scale temporal dynamics while maintaining computational efficiency. The features from the two branches are then adaptively fused through AFAM, enhancing feature complementarity and reducing noise interference. Finally, the fused features pass through a dropout layer and an activation function, followed by a fully connected layer to generate the fault classification results. The model is described in detail in the following subsections.

UAV flight sequences frequently exhibit complex dynamic behaviors with temporal dependencies spanning multiple time scales. Single-scale attention mechanisms often fail to simultaneously capture both rapid transient anomalies and slow-evolving degradation patterns, limiting their effectiveness in small-sample fault diagnosis scenarios. As a consequence, capturing temporal dependencies across multiple time scales remains crucial for modeling UAV flight sequences, which frequently exhibit complex dynamic behaviors. To address this challenge, we introduce MSAM, a multi-scale attention module that integrates parallel temporal convolutions with channel-wise attention mechanisms. This design enhances the capacity of the model to extract salient temporal patterns while mitigating redundant or noisy activations, thereby improving the robustness and discriminability of sequence representations.

3.7. AFAM

Although GDE architectures excel at capturing global temporal dependencies and DGM models effectively represent spatial local topologies, directly combining their outputs often causes modality misalignment due to structural heterogeneity between sequence-based and graph-based representations. To fuse local and global representations, enhance complementarity, and reduce noise and redundancy, we design AFAM to enable deep interactions across modalities, thus bridging global sequence modeling and localized spatial representations. AFAM comprises two main components: a cross-channel attention mechanism that captures inter-modal channel dependencies and a spatial attention mechanism that enhances localized features. This hierarchical design supports the fusion of complementary features across the GDE and DGM branches. The overall architecture of AFAM is depicted in Fig. 3.

3.8. Time complexity analysis

In this subsection, we analyze the framework's time complexity according to its data flow. The architecture comprises four primary modules: DGM, GDE, MSAM, and AFAM. Given an input feature map $X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times T}$ , with $B$ denoting batch size, $C$ channel count (or embedding dimension), and $T$ temporal sequence length, each module's time complexity is evaluated as follows.

First, the DGM module dynamically captures topological relationships among graph nodes by computing a dynamic adjacency matrix through pairwise operations over node embeddings, incurring $O(BN^{2})$ . Multi-order GCN layers then propagate features across the graph, adding $O(BN^{2})$ from dense matrix multiplications. Gating and linear transformations incur minor overhead, so the dominant complexity of DGM remains $O(BN^{2})$ .

Thereafter, GDE models long-range temporal dependencies across the sequence. Its multi-head attention mechanism performs pairwise interactions over sequence elements, resulting in $O(BT^{2}D)$ per layer. Each FFN layer incurs $O(BTDF)$ , where F represents the FFN hidden dimension. With num\_layers stacked GDE blocks, the overall time complexity of this module is $O(\text{num_layers} \times (BT^{2}D + BTD^{2} + BTDF))$ .

Subsequently, the MSAM module enhances temporal modeling via multi-scale convolutions and attention mechanisms. In particular, multiple 1D convolution branches with distinct kernel sizes extract multi-scale features, yielding a complexity of $O(BC^{2} T)$ . Additional components—channel attention and spatial attention—contribute minor terms that do not alter the overall complexity order. Thus, the primary time complexity of this module remains $O(BC^{2} T)$ .

Finally, the AFAM module integrates two input sequences using dual attention mechanisms. The channel-wise cross-attention computation requires $O(BC^{3})$ operations due to batch-wise matrix multiplications. Applying the attention maps to the sequences requires $O(BC^{2}T)$ , where

The experiments were performed on a Linux server using Python 3.12.9, CUDA 11.8, an NVIDIA RTX A10 GPU with 24 GB GRAM, and PyTorch 2.6.0 as the fault diagnosis framework. text: 4.4. Methods for comparison

We evaluated the proposed DGMANet model for FW-UAV fault diagnosis by comparing it with several representative traditional machine learning and deep learning methods. These methods have demonstrated competitive performance in UAV state recognition and fault diagnosis scenarios.
\- SVM [16]: A supervised learning algorithm widely used for binary and multi-class classification problems, particularly effective for small-scale datasets.
\- CANN [43]: A model that integrates spatial and channel attention mechanisms within a CNN to extract diverse fault features, thereby enhancing fault diagnosis performance.

\- SHNN [18]: A hybrid architecture combining 1D CNN and LSTM to extract spatial and temporal features from flight data, respectively. This approach is specifically designed for small-sample FW-UAV fault diagnosis tasks.

\- ASN [21]: A twin-tower network comprising two feature extractors with shared weights. The model adaptively reweights channel-wise features to mitigate inter-channel coupling, thus improving performance on limited training data.

\- NDDR-CNN [44]: This architecture performs discriminative dimensionality reduction via 1D convolution, batch normalization, and weight decay, followed by end-to-end training. It functions as an advanced multi-task learning (MTL) framework.
\- Cross-stitch [45]: A representative MTL model that employs cross-stitch units to optimize the combination of shared and task-specific representations across convolutional networks.

\- HDMTL [22]: A heterogeneous MTL framework combining CNN and LSTM to extract spatial and temporal features, respectively. It further employs an Adaptive Sharing Unit (ASU) to integrate complementary knowledge across feature channels, thereby enabling effective spatiotemporal learning for small-sample FW–UAV fault diagnosis.
\- MFFTD [26]: MFFTD merges spatio-temporal flight data characteristics with dynamic graph structures, employing a mutual information fusion network to address feature heterogeneity.

From a task-type perspective, SVM and CANN serve as classical machine learning and deep learning baselines, respectively, and constitute single-task learning (STL) approaches. SHNN and ASN are meta-learning-based STL methods tailored to small-sample UAV fault diagnosis. However, their reliance on episodic training and support-query matching renders them vulnerable to the scarcity of representative support samples under complex flight conditions. NDDR-CNN, Cross-Stitch, and HDMTL are advanced MTL frameworks that exploit shared spatiotemporal features to enhance generalization and robustness, yet they do not explicitly address the dynamic evolution of spatiotemporal dependencies induced by varying flight regimes. MFFTD represents a dynamic graph-based approach but separates spatial and temporal modeling into independent branches, lacking effective synergy to simultaneously capture transient fault impulses and long-term dynamic drifts. In contrast, DGMANet directly models adaptive spatiotemporal dependencies through an integrated architecture without requiring support sample constraints, thereby achieving targeted and efficient small-sample fault diagnosis for fixed-wing UAVs.

In the previous section, we validated the effectiveness of DGMANet for fault diagnosis using 90 training instances. Considering that fault data volume can influence detection performance, this section examines the performance of DGMANet across varied training sample sizes. Specifically, we assess whether the model maintains superior performance when trained on larger datasets with more comprehensive fault-related information. To this end, experiments were conducted with training sizes of 90, 120, 150, 180, 270, 360, 720, and 1440 samples. Tables 5 and 6 summarize the binary classification performance of various methods on the July 12 and 13 datasets under different training sample sizes. As the results demonstrate, the proposed DGMANet consistently outperforms all baseline methods, achieving 94.50 % and 94.24 % accuracy on the July 12 and 13 datasets with only 90 samples, and improving to 99.39 % and 99.15 % with 1440 samples. Notably, DGMANet attains Macro-F1 scores of 94.77 % and 91.58 % with only 90 samples, along with AUROC values of 98.67 % and 98.22 %, which demonstrates its superior discriminative capability and balanced diagnostic performance across all decision thresholds. This advantage derives from its effective leveraging of spatial topological dependencies among variables and its capture of long-range temporal relationships, rather than solely fusing spatial and temporal features. Among the comparison methods, HDMTL and Cross-Stitch employ multi-task learning strategies that facilitate shared representations across temporal and spatial domains, yielding competitive performance. MFFTD integrates multi-scale feature fusion for temporal dynamics modeling and demonstrates stable performance across both branches. 4.8. Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis

In this section, we evaluate the sensitivity of DGMANet to key training hyperparameters, including the learning rate, batch size, and dropout rate, which are critical for both optimization dynamics and generalization. A univariate control strategy was adopted in which each hyperparameter was independently varied within a predefined range while the others were held constant. Table 11 summarizes ranges and optimal values, and Fig. 14 presents results across four datasets.

The experimental results indicate that a learning rate of $2 \times 10^{-5}$ attains the best balance between convergence speed and generalization. Higher rates (e.g., $1 \times 10^{-4}$ ) result in unstable training and reduced performance on datasets, whereas low rates (e.g., $1 \times 10^{-5}$ ) hinder convergence. Regarding batch size, the model performs best with a value of 4. Although a smaller batch size (e.g., 2) occasionally yields competitive results, it exhibits higher variance and lower robustness; conversely, increasing the batch size to 8 results in degradation owing to reduced gradient noise and less effective regularization.

The dropout rate proves pivotal in controlling overfitting. A moderate value of 0.3 delivers stable, high accuracy across datasets, whereas lower values fail to sufficiently regularize the model and higher values (e.g., 0.5) lead to underfitting and degraded performance. Overall, these findings demonstrate that DGMANet exhibits robust performance across hyperparameter settings, and the optimal configuration reliably transfers to different data distributions.
5. Conclusions

To address the dual challenges of scarce fault samples and complex spatiotemporal dependency modeling in fault diagnosis for FW-UAV under limited data conditions, this paper introduces a novel data-driven framework, DGMANet. However, unlike traditional single-scale feature extraction methods, the proposed model fully exploits the spatiotemporal correlations in UAV flight data by jointly modeling localized topological structures and hierarchical temporal patterns. To capture spatial structure, DGMANet constructs a dynamic graph that learns adaptive inter-variable relationships. A multi-scale attention encoder extracts global temporal dependencies at multiple resolutions. An adaptive feature aggregation module fuses local and global representations, enhancing feature complementarity while suppressing redundancy. In contrast to existing approaches that overlook structural priors or temporal resolution, DGMANet integrates both spatial and temporal cues, producing more expressive and robust feature representations. Extensive experiments on four real-world FW-UAV datasets demonstrated its superior diagnostic performance and robust generalization in small-sample scenarios. However, the model has several limitations. First, its high computational complexity may constrain real-time deployment on resource-limited embedded systems. Second, its generalization across different UAV platforms, sensor configurations, and extreme environmental conditions requires further validation. Moreover, the effectiveness of the model depends on the quality and representativeness of training samples, which might not encompass all rare fault patterns encountered in practice. Future research will prioritize simplifying the model architecture to reduce computational costs while preserving accuracy, incorporating interpretability to enhance transparency in safety-critical applications, and exploring transfer learning approaches to improve cross-platform generalization with minimal retraining overhead. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be further integrated with advanced sensing technologies and multi-modal data fusion methods to enhance the robustness and real-time performance of the model, thereby more effectively satisfying the highly practical requirements of FW-UAV safe flight missions.
